| [NOTE-779](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-779.md) | Kanerva — Sparse Distributed Memory and Related Models | SDM is a two-layer memory: a fixed random address matrix selects a few of many hard locations near the cue, and an outer-product contents matrix stores the word there. | [NOTE-843](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-843.md) | Gebhart, Hansen and Schrater — Knowledge Sheaves | A knowledge-graph embedding is a knowledge sheaf on the schema (one pair of restriction maps per relation type) with a 0-cochain of its pullback to the graph. Since the zero cochain is always a section, training needs negative triples and a margin. | [NOTE-904](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-904.md) | Dar, Franklin, Jónsson, Srivastava & Tan — Semantic data caching and replacement | A client cache described by the selection predicates of past queries can answer a new selection query partly from cache (the probe query, Q ∧ V) and fetch only the rest from the server (the remainder query, Q ∧ ¬V), and can evict by semantic region rather than by page or tuple. | [NOTE-905](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-905.md) | Indyk & Motwani — Approximate nearest neighbors: towards removing the curse of dimensionality | Approximate nearest-neighbour search in d dimensions reduces, with small overhead, to a decision problem (is there a point within r, or none within (1+ε)r), and that decision problem is solved by locality-sensitive hashing: if hash functions make near pairs collide with probability at least p1 and far pairs with at most p2, then n^ρ random hash tables with ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2) answer queries with O(n^ρ) hash evaluations in O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space, with constant success probability. For Hamming space by bit sampling, and for ℓ_p with p in [1, 2] by embedding, ρ ≤ 1/(1+ε) in the 1999 text (1/ε, for ε > 1, in STOC). The paper also gives the other end of the trade: Õ(d) query time for n·O(1/ε)^d or (nd)^{O(1)} preprocessing. It is an upper bound only: it proves no lower bound, does not claim its exponents are best, solves only the approximate problem with constant probability, and counts preprocessing as space. | Read |
| [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md) | Cho & Garcia-Molina — Synchronizing a database to improve freshness (SIGMOD 2000) | For a local copy of N items, each changing as an independent Poisson process with a known rate and refreshed at fixed intervals under a fixed total refresh rate, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy fresher and younger on average than refreshing in proportion to change rate, under any distribution of rates (proved in the technical report by convexity). The freshness-optimal allocation is neither: it rises and then falls with change rate, and gives no refresh at all to items that change too fast for the budget, while the age-optimal allocation rises slowly with change rate. On estimates from 270 web sites, proportional, uniform and optimal refresh give freshness 0.12, 0.57 and 0.62. Every item matters equally, staleness is a time average with no access or query model, the refresh budget is fixed rather than priced, and refresh, change and its detection are free of any other cost. | Read |
| [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md) | Indyk & Xu — Worst-case performance of popular approximate nearest neighbor search implementations | For DiskANN's "slow preprocessing" graph (each point linked to the points that survive α-pruning of all other points, naively O(n³) time), greedy search from any start with no backtracking reaches a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) steps, each costing O((4α)^d log ∆) for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆; the ratio is tight and the dependence on ∆ cannot be replaced by log n. | [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) | Malkov & Yashunin — Hierarchical navigable small world graphs for approximate nearest neighbour search | HNSW is a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data. Each element's top layer is drawn from a geometric distribution, and new neighbours are chosen by a pruning rule that favours diverse directions. Searching from the sparse top layer down makes per-query cost grow about logarithmically with N on uniform random data in 4 and 8 dimensions, which flat NSW graphs did not. The logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded mean degree, which HNSW does not build. For the graphs it does build, logarithmic scaling is measured, at low dimension only, and on 200M SIFT vectors the paper reports the scaling "deviates from the pure logarithm". The neighbour-selection rule is what keeps clustered data searchable: in the paper's synthetic test with 100 isolated clusters, linking each element to its nearest neighbours fails to reach high recall. There is no worst-case or recall guarantee, no deletion, and no analysis of query distributions unlike the data. | Read |
| [NOTE-917](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-917.md) | Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan & Shaft — When is "nearest neighbor" meaningful? | For a fixed number n of data points and a query drawn independently of them, if the variance of the p-th power of the query-to-point distance, divided by its mean, goes to zero as dimension m grows, then the farthest point is, with probability tending to one, within any factor 1 + ε of the nearest (Theorem 1). The condition holds for IID dimensions and for several correlated or non-identical workloads, and fails when data and queries lie on a low-dimensional subspace or when queries fall inside well-separated clusters. Simulations put the collapse of contrast within 10 to 20 dimensions for IID data, and two real image-feature sets showed weak contrast. The condition is sufficient, not shown necessary; the theorem is about the ratio of distances with n held fixed, and says nothing about real data of low intrinsic dimension except that such data can escape it. | Read |
| [NOTE-918](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-918.md) | Andoni, Laarhoven, Razenshteyn & Waingarten — Optimal hashing-based time–space trade-offs for approximate near neighbors | For c-approximate near-neighbour search (find a point within cr when one lies within r) over n points in Euclidean space, the paper gives a data structure for every pair of exponents with c²√ρq + (c²−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c²−1), using space n^{1+ρu+o(1)} + O(dn) and query time n^{ρq+o(1)} + dn^{o(1)}, on worst-case data (for Hamming and ℓ_1, c√ρq + (c−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c−1)). | [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md) | Kleinberg — The small-world phenomenon: an algorithmic perspective | On an n × n lattice where each node also gets q long-range links drawn with probability proportional to d^(−r), short paths exist for r = 0, but no algorithm that sees only the links of nodes the message has visited finds them faster than about n^(2/3) steps in expectation. At r = 2 the greedy rule (pass to the contact nearest the target in lattice distance) delivers in O((log n)²) expected steps (proved for p = q = 1); for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such algorithm needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))). So efficient decentralized search depends on how the long-range links are distributed relative to the lattice, not on the links' existence or on the graph's diameter. The k-dimensional version (r = k) is stated without proof, and the model is a lattice with a known distance that every node can compute to the target. | Read |
| [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md) | Fagin, Lotem & Naor — Optimal aggregation algorithms for middleware | Given m lists of the same N objects, each sorted by one attribute's grade, and a monotone function combining the grades, the threshold algorithm (TA) reads the lists in parallel, random-accesses each newly seen object's other grades, and stops once k seen objects score at least the combined score of the last grades read. It is correct for every monotone combining function, needs constant buffers, and is instance optimal among correct algorithms that make no "wild guesses": on every database its cost is within a constant factor of any such algorithm's, the factor being m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, which is best possible when the combining function is strict (conjunction-like). Without the no-wild-guesses restriction no algorithm is instance optimal, and the counterexample is a two-list conjunction whose target sits in the middle of both lists, which any algorithm must search linearly. Fagin's Algorithm's sublinear cost O(N^((m−1)/m) k^(1/m)) is cited from Fagin, not proved here, and holds only when the lists' orderings are probabilistically independent. The model prices queries over a given set of single-attribute sorted lists. It does not price building or keeping the lists, choosing an arrangement, or any computation beyond accesses. | Read |

| [NOTE-1740](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1740.md) | Davoudabadi, Makui and Rasouli — Introducing a predictive-oriented multi-stakeholder recommender system model | The authors propose a recommender that scores each candidate item for a user by combining (a) a user-side score and (b) an organization-side score. | [NOTE-1742](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1742.md) | Gauthier and others — The political effects of X’s feed algorithm | An independent field experiment (no cooperation from X), July–September 2023. YouGov recruited active US X users; 6,043 completed the pre-survey and 4,965 the post-survey. Each was randomized, with equal probability, to X's algorithmic ("For you") or chronological ("Following") feed for about 7 weeks. Because 76% had been on the algorithmic feed beforehand and 24% on the chronological, this gives two experiments: switching the algorithm on (for initially-chronological users) and switching it off (for initially-algorithmic users). Switching it on raised engagement and moved policy priorities, views of the Trump investigations, and views of the war in Ukraine in a conservative direction (about 0.08–0.12 s.d.); switching it off had no comparable effect. A Chrome extension captured feeds: the algorithm promotes engaging, political and especially conservative content, demotes news-organization posts (−58%) and promotes political activists (+27%) and entertainment. Using scraped follow lists (n = 2,387), switching on led users to follow more conservative and conservative-activist accounts; switching off did not change follows. The authors propose that follows formed under the algorithm persist and keep feeding the chronological feed, explaining the asymmetry and the null of Meta's 2020 switch-off study. | Read |
| [NOTE-1748](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1748.md) | Scalco, Gesualdo, Cerqueti and Cinelli (2026) — How to detect information voids using longitudinal data from social media and web searches | Treating the online information ecosystem as a market with information **demand** (Wikipedia page views, Google Trends) and **supply** (Facebook posts via CrowdTangle, Twitter full-archive, GDELT news volume), the authors rescale each series by its mean, define an information delta δt = ŝt − d̂t, decompose δ by STL and flag remainder outliers by an IQR rule. Anomalies with δ < 0 are **voids** (demand far exceeds supply), δ > 0 **overabundance**; a five-regime scale runs Void / Lack / Balance / Abundance / Overabundance. On synthetic Gaussian series with injected spikes the detector reaches mean precision > 90% above 6σ. Applied to five COVID-19 vaccine brands in six European countries (Jan 2020 – Apr 2021), anomalies cluster at the vaccine rollout, at EMA's Moderna authorization and at the AstraZeneca suspension; voids outlast overabundance (up to 29 consecutive days vs 26). Matching shared URLs to NewsGuard scores, void periods carry fewer posts from top-credibility sources and more from "proceed with maximum caution" sources than non-anomalous periods. | Read |

| [NOTE-1774](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1774.md) | Hu, Jagadeesan, Jordan, Steinhardt — Incentivizing High-Quality Content in Online Recommender Systems | A game-theoretic model of a recommender platform that runs an online-learning (adversarial linear contextual bandit) algorithm, recommending one producer per arriving user, while P non-myopic, discounting producers choose a D-dimensional content vector at every step, paying cost \|\|p\|\|^c and earning 1 when recommended. Content quality is measured as producer effort \|\|p\|\| and as user welfare E[<u, p>]. For the standard no-regret algorithms LinHedge and LinEXP3, equilibrium effort (and so welfare) is bounded by a quantity that vanishes as t grows under typical learning-rate schedules. The cause is slowness: with a small learning rate, today's effort moves future recommendation probability little, and discounted producers do not find it worth paying for. The authors then design "punishment" algorithms, removing a producer for good once its content falls below a threshold (PunishHedge, PunishLinDirectionHedge), which sustain constant effort, and PunishUserUtility, which assigns individualized criteria so producers specialize, reaching near-optimal welfare in limiting cases. | Read |

| [NOTE-1787](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1787.md) | Montero-Porras, Smets and Lenaerts (2026) — Enshittification of Algorithmic Recommendation: An Evolutionary Model of Platform-Creator Dynamics | A two-population evolutionary game between a platform (x = probability its recommender rewards costly quality content) and creators (y = probability a creator invests in quality), under replicator dynamics: ẋ = x(1−x)(Ry−A), ẏ = y(1−y)(Vx−C). With R > A and V > C there are two stable pure equilibria, (1,1) "virtuous" and (0,0) "vicious", separated by an interior saddle at (x*, y*) = (C/V, A/R). Calibrated at R=1, A=0.8, V=1, C=0.5, the saddle is (0.5, 0.8): creators need the platform to reward quality half the time, but the platform needs 80% of creators investing, so the platform is "the more fragile actor" and most of the state space collapses. A temporary rise in A (to 1.2) models a lure to extraction (more lucrative ads, less moderation): if it lasts long enough for x to fall below 0.5, restoring A=0.8 does not restore quality; the system goes to (0,0). The critical shock duration rises with the platform's health at onset (convex boundary), so early intervention buys more. Conclusions add that generative AI raises A (cheaper content, costlier moderation), that content velocity may be an observable fragility proxy, and that escaping (0,0) may need joint changes of platform policy and creator participation. | Read |
| [NOTE-1792](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1792.md) | Étienne Brown — Recommended Selves: Authenticity and Algorithmic Filtering | Brown argues that recommender systems affect users' capacity to be their authentic selves, both negatively and positively. He offers a "minimal", multi-dimensional account of authenticity with two dimensions: volitional alignment (Frankfurt, via Rings: acting on first-order desires one reflectively endorses at second order) and self-understanding (an epistemic dimension, relational rather than purely introspective: others' testimony and recommendations are a source of self-knowledge). Recommenders frustrate volitional alignment "by design", because they rank on behavioural signals (clicks, dwell time) that, following Sen, cannot reveal second-order desires; the manipulation and digital-addiction literatures (Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum; Allcott, Gentzkow and Song) are cited as two forms of this. But recommenders can foster self-understanding by showing users whom they behave like (the Hao and Ellie House cases, users realizing their bisexuality), against Doyle's objection to "listening to algorithms", which Brown limits to pure deference. Opacity is the danger: the Farah case, where content is recommended for location not behaviour and she draws a false conclusion about herself. Remedies: user control (surveys, middleware, conversational recommenders, LLM "attention guardians") for volitional alignment, and explainable recommenders that say which similarity relation drove a recommendation, for self-understanding; with a tension: too much control may remove the encounters that prompt self-discovery. | Read |

Each new interaction becomes a "note" with the raw content, a timestamp, LLM-generated keywords, tags and a contextual description, and an embedding. On insertion the system retrieves the top-k most similar notes and asks an LLM which to link to (link generation), then asks an LLM whether to rewrite those neighbours' context, keywords and tags in light of the new note (memory evolution); the evolved note **replaces** the old one. | Read |
| [NOTE-1858](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1858.md) | Jiménez Gutiérrez et al. — HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models | - **Approach.** HippoRAG is a retrieval method for LLMs modelled on Teyler and Discenna's hippocampal memory indexing theory. It has two phases: - Offline: an LLM extracts open-IE triples from every passage into a schemaless knowledge graph, the "hippocampal index". Retrieval encoders add synonymy edges. - Online: named entities are extracted from the query and linked to nodes of the graph. | Read |
| [NOTE-1873](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1873.md) | Thorne, Vlachos, Christodoulopoulos and Mittal — FEVER: a large-scale dataset for Fact Extraction and VERification | FEVER is a dataset of 185,445 claims made by altering sentences from the introductions of about 50,000 popular Wikipedia pages (June 2017 dump). Altered means paraphrase, negation, entity or relation substitution, generalization and specialization. A second annotation pass, without sight of the source sentence, labelled each claim SUPPORTED, REFUTED or NOTENOUGHINFO and recorded the evidence sentences for the first two. | Read |
| [NOTE-1874](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1874.md) | Edge et al. — From Local to Global: A GraphRAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization | GraphRAG answers "global" questions about a whole corpus ("What are the main themes in the dataset?"), which ordinary vector RAG cannot, because retrieving the top-k similar chunks samples the corpus instead of summarizing it. At index time an LLM extracts entities, relationships and "claims" from text chunks, merges them into a knowledge graph (exact string matching for entity names), partitions the graph hierarchically with Leiden community detection, and pre-generates a report-like summary for every community at every level. At query time each community summary yields a partial answer with a 0–100 helpfulness score (map), and the best partial answers are summarized into a global answer (reduce). | Read |
| [NOTE-1887](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1887.md) | Park et al. — Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior | The paper builds LLM-driven agents that simulate believable everyday human behaviour in a Sims-like town of 25 agents. Its architecture has three parts: a memory stream (a timestamped list of natural-language observations), retrieval scored by recency, importance (LLM-rated poignancy) and relevance (embedding similarity), and reflection, in which the agent periodically asks itself high-level questions, retrieves memories and writes "insights" that cite the memories they came from; reflections go back into the stream and can be reflected on, forming trees. Planning sits on top. | Skimmed |
